Expectation1: Adhere to site protocols and work effectively as part of the team.
Situation1: A notice has been posted about an optional training session happening next week.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I wiped the sweat from my brow, glancing at the notice tacked to the breakroom wall: “Optional Safety Training—Next Week.” The foreman had already mentioned how important it was for everyone to show up, even if it wasn’t mandatory. “We need to look out for each other,” he’d said, and I knew he was right. The crew counted on me to pull my weight, to be there, to follow the protocols that kept us safe. But as I scrolled through my phone during lunch, a message popped up from the advocacy group: a local worker had just faced blatant discrimination at a nearby site. They needed someone to speak out, to organize a response, to make sure this didn’t get swept under the rug. My heart pounded. I was expected to be the voice for those who couldn’t speak, to shine a light on injustice. But if I missed the training, I’d let my team down. If I ignored the call for advocacy, I’d betray my own values. I stared at the notice, torn between two worlds, feeling the weight of both pressing down on me.
